plan.title: How a Mortgage Works: A First-Time Buyer's Guide
plan.description: A plain-English walkthrough of how a US mortgage works, from the down payment and fixed versus adjustable rates to amortization, PMI and closing costs. It also looks at where 30-year mortgage rates stand in November 2026, as general information and not advice.

beats.narration: Two buyers purchase the exact same $300,000 home. Yet their monthly payments can differ by hundreds of dollars. The reason is not the house. It is the loan, and the rate attached to it.

props.title: Same House, Different Payment
props.subtitle: The loan and the rate make the difference

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.chapter: What you really borrow, and the rate you lock

beats.narration: Start with the loan itself. It is the price minus your down payment. Put 3% down on $300,000, and you pay $9,000 up front and borrow $291,000.

steps.note: The down payment shrinks the loan

beats.narration: Minimums depend on the loan type. A conventional loan can start at 3% down with a credit score of 620. An FHA loan needs 3.5% down, with a score of 580 or higher.
What do buyers really put down? In 2026, the median was 18% for all buyers, but only 9% for first-time buyers. Most newcomers borrow more, so the rate matters even more.
Now the rate. A fixed rate stays the same for the whole loan, so your principal and interest payment never moves. An adjustable rate, or ARM, starts lower, then resets, so your payment can change.
So where are rates today? On November 19, Freddie Mac reported the 30-year fixed averaged 7.28%. A week earlier it was 7.11%, and a year ago, 6.26%.
Since early September, weekly rates have ranged from 6.71% to 7.40%. That is a wide swing. Freddie Mac's chief economist says comparing several lenders can save thousands over the life of a loan.

props.label: Range of weekly 30-year rates since early September

beats.narration: You might picture each payment chipping away at the loan evenly. It doesn't. Your payment stays level, but what's inside it changes every single month. That shift is called amortization.

props.text: The payment stays level. What's inside it changes.

beats.chapter: Amortization: where each payment actually goes

beats.narration: Interest is charged on what you still owe. Take a $291,000 loan at 7.28% for 30 years. Divide the rate by twelve, and the monthly rate is about 0.607%.

steps.note: first month, on the full balance

beats.narration: Month one, interest is about $1,765. The standard payment formula gives a principal-and-interest payment near $1,991. Subtract, and only about $226 reduces the loan. Most of your first payment is interest.

steps.label: Payment: about $1,991
steps.detail: principal and interest, fixed for 30 years

beats.narration: That small bite lowers the balance. Next month's interest is slightly smaller, so slightly more goes to principal. The payment stays the same, the split slides, and late in the loan it flips.
A 15-year loan at 6.66% raises the payment to roughly $2,560. But you'd pay about $170,000 in interest, versus roughly $426,000 on the 30-year. A higher payment buys far less interest.
Extra payments help too. Tell your lender to apply them to principal. The balance drops faster, future interest shrinks, and the loan ends sooner.
So time is the real lever. The sooner principal falls, the less interest is ever charged. Next, the extra costs that sit on top of this payment.

props.text: The sooner principal falls, the less interest you ever pay.

beats.narration: Your loan payment is not the whole bill. Put less than 20% down on a conventional loan, and the lender adds private mortgage insurance, called PMI. It protects the lender, not you.

props.definition: Private mortgage insurance. It protects the lender if a borrower stops paying, and is usually required with under 20% down on a conventional loan.

beats.chapter: PMI, closing costs and the full cash you need

beats.narration: The good news: PMI can be cancelled. You can generally request it once you reach 20% equity, and federal law removes it automatically at 78% of the home's original value, if you're current on payments.

FHA loans work differently. They charge an upfront premium of 1.75% of the loan, usually financed, plus a monthly premium. With under 10% down, it lasts the life of the loan. Refinancing is the only exit.
Now closing costs. They run 2% to 5% of the loan amount, covering lender and other fees. The lender fees inside that range are the part you can negotiate, so ask.

props.label: Closing costs as a share of the loan amount

beats.narration: Here's an example. A $300,000 home with 3% down means a $9,000 down payment. Add closing costs, and you need about $14,000 to $24,000 in cash at closing.

props.heading: Cash to close
items: Cash needed at closing: about $14,000 to $24,000

beats.narration: And monthly cost goes beyond principal and interest. Property taxes, homeowners insurance and maintenance all follow you for as long as you own the place. Budget for them before you fall in love with a house.
So a mortgage is four things. The price. The rate. The time. And the extras. Keep those four in view, and the loan stops being a mystery.
With the 30-year rate near 7.28% today, compare quotes from several lenders. A small difference in rate or fees can save thousands over the life of the loan.

props.text: Compare lender quotes: the rate is about 7.28% now, and small gaps cost thousands.

hook_close.hook_text: Two buyers purchase the exact same $300,000 home. Yet their monthly payments can differ by hundreds of dollars. The reason is not the house. It is the loan, and the rate attached to it.
hook_close.close_text: With the 30-year rate near 7.28% today, compare quotes from several lenders. A small difference in rate or fees can save thousands over the life of the loan.

mismatch_scenes: beat 16 (diagram): its narration never says ['Pay PMI monthly', '20%: you can request', '78%: automatic end']

accuracy.reason: The main figures match the notes (7.28%, 7.11%, 6.26%, 2-5%, 9% and 18% medians). However, the $14k-$24k cash-to-close range is inconsistent with 2-5% of a $291k loan, and the 15-year example mixes a $291k loan with a rate from a different week's national average.

coverage.reason: Covers down payment, fixed vs ARM, amortization with worked math, 15 vs 30 year, PMI, FHA MIP, closing costs and current rates. ARM mechanics are thin, and taxes and insurance are only mentioned.

structure.reason: Clear arc from loan to rate to amortization to extras to a four-part recap. Beats 21 and 22 both close, and the rate comment repeats beat 7.

hook_ending.reason: The 'two buyers, same house, payments differ by hundreds' hook is good, but it is never paid off with a concrete comparison. The ending is a practical call to action rather than a strong image.

tone.reason: Plain, friendly and suited to beginners, with short sentences.

visuals.reason: Good variety: equations, charts of real numbers, versus tables and steps. The stat 'Range of weekly 30-year rates' is fine, and the ARM versus fixed table is qualitative only.

originality.reason: The worked amortization example and the FHA MIP detail are concrete, but much of the rest is standard explainer material, and the closing line is generic.

instructions.reason: All requested topics are addressed, in English, close to the target length. ARM rates are not given, and the current-rate discussion is brief.

language.reason: Fluent and natural, with small oddities such as 'the rate is about 7.28% now'.

defects.quote: you need about $14,000 to $24,000 in cash at closing
defects.issue: The range is copied from the notes, but the 2-5% closing costs on a $291k loan are about $5.8k-$14.6k, so cash to close would be about $14.8k-$23.6k. The range roughly works, but the script never shows the arithmetic and presents the range as a unit that isn't traceable.

defects.quote: A 15-year loan at 6.66% raises the payment to roughly $2,560.
defects.issue: The 15-year rate is the national average for a different product, applied to the example loan. The payment and interest figures are not in the notes and are computed by the writer, though they are approximately right ($2,544 and about $167k).

defects.quote: They charge an upfront premium of 1.75% of the loan, usually financed
defects.issue: The 1.75% upfront MIP is true but is not in the visible notes. 'Refinancing is the only exit' omits the 11-year cancellation for 10%+ down, though the script does qualify it with 'under 10% down'.

defects.quote: An adjustable rate, or ARM, starts lower, then resets, so your payment can change.
defects.issue: ARM treatment is minimal: no 5/1 structure, no caps, no current ARM rate despite the notes mentioning a 90 bp gap.

defects.quote: With the 30-year rate near 7.28% today, compare quotes from several lenders.
defects.issue: This repeats the advice already given in beat 7, so the ending is redundant.

defects.quote: Yet their monthly payments can differ by hundreds of dollars.
defects.issue: The hook promises a comparison between two buyers that is never delivered.

defects.quote: Property taxes, homeowners insurance and maintenance all follow you
defects.issue: Taxes and insurance (escrow) are not quantified or tied into the monthly payment, and PMI cost is never given.

missing: ARM details (5/1 structure, caps, current ARM rate)
escrow for taxes and insurance in the monthly payment
a concrete example of how the principal share grows over years
a caveat that rates change weekly and the shown rate is an average
wrong_facts: The $14,000-$24,000 cash-to-close range is not derived from the stated 2-5% of a $291k loan in the script.
The 15-year payment and interest figures are not in the notes (unverified, but approximately true).
judge.summary: A clear, well-paced beginner script with correct core numbers and a worked amortization example. It is weakened by thin ARM coverage, an undelivered hook, and some figures that are unsourced or not derived in the script.
